questions.q: Name the three sub-phases of the Palaeolithic Period in chronological order and give one characteristic tool type for each phase found in the Indian subcontinent.
questions.a: Lower Palaeolithic (handaxes/cleavers), Middle Palaeolithic (scrapers/points on flakes), Upper Palaeolithic (blades/burins). A wrong answer (e.g., listing microliths for Upper Palaeolithic or missing Middle Palaeolithic) reveals the student cannot distinguish the Indian sequence from the European one or conflates Palaeolithic with later periods.

questions.q: Why did Lower Palaeolithic humans in India prefer quartzite for making handaxes and cleavers, even though flint was available in some regions?
questions.a: Quartzite is abundant in peninsular river gravels (e.g., Hunsgi, Attirampakkam) and tough enough for heavy-duty butchery; flint is rarer in the south. A wrong answer citing "flint is sharper" shows the student ignores raw material availability – a key factor in Indian Palaeolithic technology – and applies a European flint-centric model inappropriately.

questions.q: An archaeologist finds a layer with Levallois flakes and side-scrapers but no handaxes at a site near the Narmada Valley. Which Palaeolithic sub-phase does this represent, and what does the absence of handaxes suggest about the site's function?
questions.a: Middle Palaeolithic; the absence of handaxes suggests a specialized activity site (e.g., butchery or tool maintenance) rather than a base camp where large cores were reduced. A wrong answer identifying it as Upper Palaeolithic (due to "advanced" flakes) reveals confusion between Levallois technique (Middle) and blade technology (Upper) and misses the functional interpretation of tool assemblages.

questions.q: Compare the subsistence strategies implied by Lower Palaeolithic Acheulean sites (e.g., Attirampakkam) and Upper Palaeolithic sites (e.g., Bhimbetka III-F-23). What environmental change best explains the shift?
questions.a: Lower: large-game hunting/scavenging with heavy tools in open grasslands; Upper: diversified hunting (small game, fish), plant processing, and symbolic behavior in patchy forests. The shift correlates with the Last Glacial Maximum (c. 20,000 BCE) fragmenting habitats. A wrong answer attributing change solely to "better brains" ignores the climate-driven ecological restructuring documented in Indian pollen records.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The rock art at Bhimbetka proves Upper Palaeolithic humans in India had fully modern language and religion." Use archaeological evidence to support your judgment.
questions.a: The claim overreaches. Art indicates symbolic capacity, but language and religion leave no direct fossil evidence. Comparable art appears in Middle Palaeolithic contexts globally (e.g., Blombos Cave). A stronger answer notes art + ochre use + burial at Bhimbetka suggests complex culture, but "fully modern language" is inferred, not proven. A wrong answer accepting the claim uncritically shows inability to distinguish evidence from inference – a board-level source-analysis error.

questions.q: Create a three-column table comparing Lower, Middle, and Upper Palaeolithic tool kits in India. For each phase, list: (a) dominant raw material, (b) key tool types, (c) inferred primary activity, and (d) a representative Indian site.
questions.a: A good table shows: Lower – quartzite, handaxe/cleaver, large-mammal butchery, Attirampakkam; Middle – chert/quartzite, Levallois flakes/scrapers, hide/wood working, Hunsgi; Upper – chert/chalcedony, blades/burins, composite tools/art, Bhimbetka. A poor table copies European types (e.g., "Solutrean laurel leaf") or omits raw material, revealing rote memorization without understanding Indian geological constraints.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Palaeolithic Period (Old Stone Age) in the Indian subcontinent spans from approximately 2.5 million years ago to 10,000 BCE, ______ by the earliest stone tool industries (handaxes, cleavers, scrapers) made by hominins like Homo erectus and early Homo sapiens, who lived as nomadic hunter-gatherers in small bands, used fire, and created the first known rock art at sites like Bhimbetka.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are standing at the ______ rock shelters in Madhya Pradesh, looking at paintings of hunters chasing deer made 30,000 years ago.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can classify Lower, Middle, and Upper Palaeolithic tool types from images or descriptions, explain how tool technology reflects changing subsistence strategies, and correlate major Indian sites (Attirampakkam, Bhimbetka, Hunsgi) with their specific tool assemblages and environmental contexts.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Palaeolithic Period (Old Stone Age) in the Indian subcontinent spans from ______ 2.5 million years ago to 10,000 BCE, characterized by the earliest stone tool industries (handaxes, cleavers, scrapers) made by hominins like Homo erectus and early Homo sapiens, who lived as nomadic hunter-gatherers in small bands, used fire, and created the first known rock art at sites like Bhimbetka.
